name: Arginine (AAKG)

lead: AAKG is a salt of the amino acid L-arginine and alpha-ketoglutarate, marketed to lifters as a nitric oxide booster for muscle pumps, blood flow and endurance. It is a staple of pre-workout formulas.
Published human trials are few and small. Titles of several of them report that acute AAKG or arginine supplementation failed to improve muscular performance or endurance.

paras: Arginine is the precursor of nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels. The marketing idea is that more arginine means more nitric oxide, more blood flow and a bigger pump. Alpha-ketoglutarate is a metabolic intermediate and glutamine precursor. Whether the combined salt raises nitric oxide better than plain arginine is not clearly established.

Grokipedia describes AAKG as generally tolerated at 3 to 6 g daily, with mild gastrointestinal upset at higher intakes. A 2012 case report described a hemorrhagic stroke in a young man after a multi-ingredient sports supplement (Jack3d) that contained other stimulants, so the cause cannot be attributed to AAKG alone.

trials.title: Effects of a Pre-Workout Dietary Supplement on Training Adaptations

lead: Arginine alpha-ketoglutarate (AAKG) is a dietary supplement made of the amino acid L-arginine paired with alpha-ketoglutaric acid, typically in a 2:1 molar ratio, and marketed as more soluble or bioavailable than arginine alone.[1] It is sold mainly to athletes and bodybuilders as a pre-workout ingredient intended to raise nitric oxide, improve muscle blood flow and increase strength or endurance.[1]

Arginine is the sole precursor of nitric oxide in humans, a molecule that relaxes vascular smooth muscle.[2] That physiology is the basis for the supplement's marketing, but controlled trials in trained and untrained men have generally not found a performance benefit from acute AAKG or arginine.[3][4]

paras: AAKG is sold as a stand-alone powder or capsule and as an ingredient in multi-ingredient pre-workout products. Proponents claim it supports muscle pumps during resistance training, aids recovery and promotes ammonia handling through the urea cycle.[1]

L-arginine is a semi-essential amino acid that nitric oxide synthases convert into nitric oxide; its relative ADMA inhibits that production.[2] Alpha-ketoglutarate is an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle.[1] Grokipedia states that neither plain arginine nor AAKG is clearly superior for enhancing nitric oxide production or muscle outcomes.[1]
A pharmacokinetic study in 10 healthy men compared time-released and non-time-released 4 g AAKG and tracked plasma arginine over 8 hours.[5]

A 2006 randomized, double-blind study in trained men evaluated the pharmacokinetics, safety and exercise effects of AAKG.[5] A 2012 trial reported that acute AAKG supplementation failed to improve muscular performance in resistance-trained and untrained men, and a 2011 study reported that acute arginine did not improve muscle endurance or alter blood pressure responses to resistance exercise.[3][4] A 2011 trial examined seven days of AAKG on blood flow, plasma arginine and nitric oxide metabolites after resistance exercise.[6]

Two 2017 studies tested a multi-ingredient pre-workout product, with and without synephrine, on exercise outcomes and training adaptations in healthy participants; because those products contain many ingredients, effects cannot be assigned to AAKG alone.[7][8]

Grokipedia reports that AAKG is generally well tolerated at 3 to 6 g daily, with nausea or diarrhea at higher intakes, and that it is not recommended for people with herpes infections or kidney problems.[1] Wikipedia lists plain L-arginine as generally recognized as safe at intakes up to 20 g per day and notes possible interactions with drugs.[2]
A 2012 military medicine case report described a hemorrhagic stroke in a young healthy man after using a multi-ingredient sports supplement, Jack3d.[9]
